t: Djenné grew from the older urban settlement of Djenné-Djeno, first occupied around 200 BCE, and the present town, settled after 1000 CE, took over as the older site was abandoned by about 1400.

Between the 15th and 17th centuries much of the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves that passed through Timbuktu also passed through Djenné, and both towns were centres of Islamic scholarship.
Sonni Ali took the town in 1471, Moroccan forces held the region after 1591, and later it passed to the Segou kingdom, the Massina Empire, the Toucouleur Empire and, in 1893, France.
dyk: Each year the floods of the Bani and Niger rivers turn Djenné into an island, reached by causeways. Its mud-brick houses must be replastered at least every other year, and the Great Mosque every year.
ev: The present town of Djenné is first settled
Sonni Ali conquers Djenné after a siege of about six months
The Songhai are defeated at Tondibi by a Moroccan army, and their empire collapses
Djenné becomes part of the Segou kingdom
René Caillié becomes the first European to visit the town
French forces under Louis Archinard occupy Djenné
UNESCO names Djenné and Djenné-Djeno a World Heritage Site

f.founded: The nearby site of Djenné-Djeno was first settled around 200 BCE according to excavations of 1977 and 1981; the present town was first settled after 1000 CE, while oral tradition dates its founding to 635 and names a legendary founder, Maafir.
f.where: On the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers at the southern end of the Inland Niger Delta in central Mali, 398 km north-east of Bamako and 76 km south-west of Mopti.
f.known: The old site of Djenné-Djeno; the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves; Islamic scholarship beside Timbuktu; the Songhai siege of 1471; the Moroccan conquest; adobe architecture; the Great Mosque
f.today: Djenné is a town and urban commune of the Mopti Region of Mali and, with Djenné-Djeno, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.
